author: arcprize
summary: ARC Prize places Argon behind Astra’s 99.9% ARC-AGI-3 result. It reports 62% fewer actions than the human baseline on the 25 public games, matching or beating three speedrun records and coming within 10% on six others.
whyItMatters: Keep the public-demo action comparison separate from the semi-private Verified score.

author: arcprize
summary: ARC Prize says API issues prevented complete standard-harness testing: low reasoning completed 42/55 games for 49.8%; medium completed 46/55 for 46.3%; high completed 19/55 and no score was published. Reported scores retain partial credit across all 55 games. Provider adapter preserves opaque reasoning and permits automatic compaction; standard harness carries notes between turns. Costs use introductory $2 input/$10 output per million tokens.
whyItMatters: Material limit on harness comparisons. Do not present incomplete standard-harness runs as a clean capability ceiling.

author: arcprize
summary: ARC Prize announces Gemini 4 Argon Verified results: ARC-AGI-3 97.5% at $4.8K with the provider adapter and 49.8% at $5.8K with the standard harness; ARC-AGI-2 91.3% at $0.32/task and ARC-AGI-1 98.5% at $0.16/task. It calls Google DeepMind the second frontier lab above 95% on ARC-AGI-3.
whyItMatters: Consequential organizer result. Separate from Kaggle standings. Standard-harness API incompletion is essential context; primary results introduction says 91.2% on v2 while its table and announcement say 91.3%.

author: arcprize
summary: ARC Prize’s October 13 announcement reports DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at about 3% with its provider adapter and below 1% with the standard harness. The original linked verified-results table, refreshed October 14, gives a matched Low-reasoning comparison of 3.26% versus 0.35%; its headline best configurations differ in reasoning level. Organizer model evaluation, separate from Kaggle team submissions.
whyItMatters: Public original read without sign-in in the in-app browser; linked primary results table independently read. Organizer evaluation, separate from Kaggle team standings.

author: arcprize
summary: ARC Prize announces Tufa Labs reclaimed first on the ARC-AGI-3 public Kaggle board with roughly 69%, up from roughly 56%. This is the author’s dated October 13 observation; refresh standings before publication.
whyItMatters: Organizer confirmation of a consequential team result already covered in the newspaper’s morning/afternoon reporting; no methods disclosed.

author: OCEANVIN10
summary: OCEAN highlighted the Memento 3 preprint. Its authors report that a fixed language model revises an external rulebook and executable world model; on the 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, they report clearing every level with fewer actions than the human baseline. These are author-reported results on the public set.
whyItMatters: A new ARC-AGI-3 research lead for the edition desk. The paper provides a concrete mechanism and results, but the public tutorial set cannot establish private-game performance.

author: mhmazur
summary: Mazur announces a new Emergent Mind homepage and a shift to an experimental product lab, with the arXiv research assistant retained as one of its tools. He says most tools will be small and free, with some larger paid tools. The actual homepage independently displays AI Product Lab by Matt Mazur and links the assistant, open problems and experimental projects.
whyItMatters: Organizer capture before editorial selection. Product and community context, not an ARC score or competition result. Each item was read at its actual permalink with no subscriber restriction.

author: iiiiitsu_ne
summary: Itsu announces a move to rank 14 in ARC-AGI-2, with a joke comparing the climb to the electricity bill. The original post links the ARC-AGI-2 competition. Chrome subsequently showed Muggle at rank 14 with nisshokuitsuki as its listed account; the collector snapshot at 09:49:46 UTC maps that account to team 16297545.
whyItMatters: Fresh contender statement for the Early edition: rank 14 is within the observed provisional public gold band. Do not imply the score was achieved at the post time or a final medal has been won.

author: nickcammarata
summary: Nick adds that agents have automated circuit-study work that previously took months for the Curve Detectors / Curve Circuits experiments on ten neurons.
whyItMatters: Attributed claim about research automation, not a measured ARC result.

author: nickcammarata
summary: Responding to Knoop, Nick says such an evaluation seems feasible and points to controlled activations, ablations, large token collections and other circuit-study tools; he promises more details.
whyItMatters: Substantive response to the organizer’s evaluation proposal. Feasibility is the author’s view.

author: mhmazur
summary: Replying to Fraser Price’s simulated multicellular-life video, Mazur praises the research but says the difficult next step is advancing beyond such demonstrations, perhaps by evolving rudimentary intelligence.
whyItMatters: Organizer commentary on open-ended research. The parent simulation claim was read but not independently validated.

author: mikeknoop
summary: Replying to Nick’s Neural Networks Are Already Clean announcement, Knoop asks whether neural-network cleanliness can be formalized as an evaluation and whether the proposed falsifiable-explanation experiment would suffice.
whyItMatters: Concrete evaluation question, with two substantive replies from the original author. No ARC score or validated new evaluation announced.

author: mikeknoop
summary: Knoop argues experiment ideation is the current bottleneck in recursive self-improvement. He claims coding and execution are largely automated, distinguishes reproducing known results from asking novel questions, and says domain-specific improvement recipes still need human-AI collaboration to spread across domains without further generalization breakthroughs.
whyItMatters: Useful organizer perspective on open-ended evaluation and ARC-AGI. His automation percentages and 12-month scenario are attributed claims, not independently verified results.

author: fchollet
summary: Chollet says Argon has a similar ARC-AGI-3 performance profile to Astra and calls Google back at the frontier, quoting ARC Prize’s result.
whyItMatters: Attributed organizer reaction to the Verified release; not a separate evaluation.

author: iiiiitsu_ne
summary: Itsu reports moving to rank 30 on Kaggle. The original post links ARC Prize 2026 - ARC-AGI-2.
whyItMatters: Dated competitor statement. Later collector snapshot at 20:48:28Z lists Odd Dice, team 16297545, roster nisshokuitsuki, at rank 32; the post is not a current-rank claim.

author: mikeknoop
summary: Knoop calls Argon the second model family effectively to max out ARC-AGI-3 with a provider adapter and notes a similar backwards bend in action efficiency.
whyItMatters: Attributed reaction; preserve the provider-adapter qualification and avoid equating it with Kaggle performance.

author: arcprize
summary: ARC Prize links the Verified leaderboard, reproducible public benchmark code, testing policy and full Gemini 4 Argon results.
whyItMatters: Primary evidence links for edition follow-up; no new Kaggle ranking.

author: harshitj__
summary: Joshi introduces SHELDON, a reasoning harness that separately tracks hypotheses and observations. His thread claims ARC-AGI-2 improvement over its baselines. The linked Stanford project table reports 59.17 for SHELDON versus 47.50 for EvoX, using GPT-5.6-terra high reasoning and GPT-5.6-luna for delegated implementation.
whyItMatters: Fresh primary research lead. These are author-reported experimental results, not Kaggle standings or an ARC Prize Verified evaluation; confirm split, budget and comparability before publication.

author: masspeakss
summary: Translation of Japanese original: An ARC2 merge invitation involving the gold range has come in, so I am torn, but I want to keep trying solo until the last possible moment. The post does not name the inviting team or announce an accepted merger.
whyItMatters: Contender motivation and possible future team change; do not report a merger or a verified gold position. Exact current team mapping remains unresolved.

author: mhmazur
summary: Replying to Vlad Garbuz’s question about the provider checkpoint used for the DeepSeek evaluation, Mazur says Baseten serves the original DeepSeek V4.1 Flash checkpoint, which natively uses fp8 with mxfp4 experts, without additional quantization. Original reply and parent chain read in regular public-post UI, with no Subscribers restriction. This is Mazur’s testing clarification, not an independently reproduced provider comparison.
whyItMatters: New organizer detail for interpreting the October 13 verified DeepSeek evaluation. Keep the native mixed precision distinct from additional provider quantization; no new Kaggle score or ruling.
